title: Look-Alike, Sound-Alike
objectives: I can tell apart five pairs of words that look or sound alike and use each one correctly.
I can use spelling and sound clues to remember which word to write.
I can use context clues to choose the right word in a sentence.
I can write sentences that use both words in a pair.
rationale: Look-alike and sound-alike pairs are among the most common errors in fourth-grade writing, and each error changes meaning (advice or advise, lose or loose). The unit teaches five pairs side by side so students notice the one-letter or one-sound difference that carries the meaning. Pairs were chosen for a teachable contrast: noun and verb with a sound change (advice/advise, breath/breathe), a spelling change that changes the meaning (lose/loose, compliment/complement), and a distance versus amount contrast (farther/further). Each pair gets a memory clue, a test sentence, and a context passage so that students choose by meaning, not by guessing.

words.def: Helpful words about what someone should do.
words.ex: My coach gave me good advice about stretching before a run.
words.ex2: Grandpa's best advice was to read the directions before starting anything.
words.nonExample: Asking what time the bus comes is a question, not advice.

apps.academic: In a how-to text, the writer often ends with advice for the reader.
apps.spoken: Thanks for the advice; I will try it.
apps.writing: Use advice as a noun, as in "She gave me advice."

cloze.s: I asked my aunt for ___ about which science book to borrow, and she picked the best one.

cloze2.s: The nurse's ___ was to drink water and rest, so Ben stayed home and slept all day.

misuse.s: My advice is a heavy red backpack that I carry to school.
misuse.why: Advice is helpful words about what to do; it is not a thing you can carry.

visual.alt: A speech bubble beside a glowing light bulb.

words.frame: The best advice I ever got was ___.

words.def: To tell someone what you think they should do.
words.ex: The librarian will advise you on which mystery book to start with.
words.ex2: Doctors advise children to sleep at least nine hours each night.
words.nonExample: Forcing a friend to follow your plan is not advising them.

apps.academic: A scientist may advise a city on how to protect a river.
apps.spoken: I advise you to wear boots today.
apps.writing: Use advise as a verb, as in "I advise you to wait."

cloze.s: The guide will ___ us to wear boots because the trail is full of sharp rocks.

cloze2.s: I ___ you to check the weather first, since storms can arrive quickly here.

misuse.s: She advised her desk to finish its math homework.
misuse.why: To advise is to tell a person what to do; a desk cannot listen or do homework.

visual.alt: A person speaking and pointing to a checklist.

words.def: To be unable to find something anymore.

senses.def: To fail to win a game or contest.
senses.example: Our team will lose if we stop passing the ball.

words.ex: Mia taped her key to a string so she would not lose it.
words.ex2: Do not lose your library card on the way home from school.
words.nonExample: Finding your missing glove under the couch is the opposite of losing it.

apps.academic: In science, a scientist should not lose the notes from an experiment.
apps.spoken: I always lose my other sock.
apps.writing: Use lose with one o; it rhymes with choose.

cloze.s: If you ___ your lunch ticket, the cashier will need a new one before you can eat.

cloze2.s: Tie the balloon tightly so you do not ___ it in the strong wind.

misuse.s: Please lose the door so the cold air stays out of the house.
misuse.why: Lose means to be unable to find something; the word for shutting a door is close.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass searching for a missing glove.

words.frame: I do not want to lose ___.

words.def: Not tight or firmly held in place.
words.ex: A loose tooth wiggled when Ana touched it with her tongue.
words.ex2: The farmer fixed the gate because the loose latch let the cows wander out.
words.nonExample: A knot pulled as tight as it will go is not loose.

apps.academic: A loose screw can make a machine shake and stop working.
apps.spoken: This jacket is a little loose on me.
apps.writing: Use loose with two o's; it has an extra o, like a loose, stretched-out word.

cloze.s: The ___ board on the porch wobbled every time someone stepped on it.

cloze2.s: Grandpa's old jacket was so ___ that it hung off his shoulders like a blanket.

misuse.s: The screw was loose, so it held the shelf firmly and nothing wobbled.
misuse.why: Loose means not tight; a loose screw cannot hold a shelf firmly.

visual.alt: A wobbly tooth next to a screw that is coming out.

words.def: At a greater distance that you can measure.
words.ex: Dev threw the ball farther than anyone else on the field.
words.ex2: My house is farther from school than yours, so I ride the bus.
words.nonExample: Wanting more details about a story is not about distance, so it is not farther.
words.rel: farther (distance) and further (more, to a greater degree)

apps.academic: Scientists measure how much farther a rocket travels with more fuel.
apps.spoken: Can you run farther than a mile?
apps.writing: Use farther when you can measure the distance in steps, feet, or miles.

cloze.s: The hikers walked ___ up the trail until the parking lot was out of sight.

cloze2.s: Our seats were ___ from the stage than we had hoped, so we brought binoculars.

misuse.s: Lila threw the ball farther than her sister, so her ball landed closer.
misuse.why: Farther means a greater distance, so the ball would land away, not closer.

visual.alt: A runner racing along a path marked with a measuring tape.

words.def: More; to a greater amount or degree.
words.ex: The detective wanted to look further into the mystery of the missing key.
words.ex2: We will talk further about the field trip after lunch.
words.nonExample: Counting how many steps it is to the door is a question about farther, not further.
words.rel: farther (distance) and further (more, to a greater degree)

apps.academic: Further research can help scientists answer the questions left over.
apps.spoken: I need to think about this further.
apps.writing: Use further when you mean more, as in further study or further questions.

cloze.s: The scientist wanted to study the bird ___ before she wrote her report.

cloze2.s: Mom said we would discuss the new puppy ___ once everyone had time to think.

misuse.s: We have nothing further to say, so we talked for two more hours.
misuse.why: Nothing further means no more; talking for two more hours contradicts that.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass beside a plus sign.

words.frame: I want to learn further about ___.

words.def: The air you take into your body and let out.
words.ex: Mina took a deep breath before she began her speech.
words.ex2: On the freezing morning, we could see our breath hanging in the air.
words.nonExample: A sneeze is not a breath, because it pushes air out hard and fast.

apps.academic: The lungs help us bring in a breath of oxygen.
apps.spoken: I'm out of breath after that race.
apps.writing: Use breath with no e at the end for the noun; it rhymes with death.

cloze.s: After the race, Jo was out of ___ and sat down on the grass to rest.

cloze2.s: Hold your ___ for five seconds while the doctor listens to your chest.

misuse.s: He bought a new breath at the store and put it in his backpack.
misuse.why: A breath is air going in or out of your body; you cannot buy one in a store.

visual.alt: A person whose breath makes a small cloud in cold air.

words.frame: I take a deep breath when ___.

words.def: To take air in and let it out.
words.ex: Swimmers learn to breathe every few strokes so they do not get tired.
words.ex2: It was hard to breathe in the smoky room, so we opened a window.
words.nonExample: Holding your air in until your chest hurts is the opposite of breathing.

apps.academic: Plants take in carbon dioxide, and animals breathe in oxygen.
apps.spoken: Just breathe and take your time.
apps.writing: Use breathe with an e at the end for the verb; it rhymes with seethe.

cloze.s: Divers carry tanks of air so they can ___ underwater for a long time.

cloze2.s: Please ___ slowly through your nose to help your heartbeat calm down.

misuse.s: The rock breathes quickly after it runs up the hill.
misuse.why: Only living things such as animals and people breathe; a rock is not alive.

visual.alt: A scuba diver with bubbles rising from the mouthpiece.

words.def: A kind thing you say about someone.
words.ex: Maya smiled at the compliment about her colorful drawing.
words.ex2: The chef accepted the compliment and thanked the customers for visiting.
words.nonExample: Making fun of someone's shirt is an insult, not a compliment.
words.rel: compliment (kind words) and complement (goes well with)

apps.academic: A good peer review begins with a compliment about the writer's strengths.
apps.writing: Remember: compliment with an i means "I like it."

cloze.s: Dad said, "That was a lovely song," and Rosa blushed at the ___.

cloze2.s: A thoughtful ___ about my hard work made me want to keep trying.

misuse.s: He gave me a compliment by saying my story was boring and too long.
misuse.why: A compliment is a kind remark; saying a story is boring is an insult.

visual.alt: A speech bubble with a gold star inside.

words.frame: A kind compliment I could give a friend is ___.

words.def: To go well with something and make it better.
words.ex: The blue scarf will complement her yellow coat.
words.ex2: A crunchy salad can complement a bowl of warm soup.
words.nonExample: Two colors that clash do not complement each other.
words.rel: compliment (kind words) and complement (goes well with)

apps.academic: In art, two colors that complement each other make a picture stand out.
apps.spoken: The sauce complements the pasta well.
apps.writing: Remember: complement with an e completes something.

cloze.s: The soft music will ___ the dim lights and make the dinner feel cozy.

cloze2.s: Green beans ___ the chicken nicely, so the plate looks and tastes balanced.

misuse.s: The loud, scratchy radio will complement the quiet library by ruining the calm.
misuse.why: To complement is to go well with and improve; ruining the calm does the opposite.

visual.alt: A blue scarf draped over a yellow coat.

passage.title: Marco's Race
paras: Before the school race, Marco's older brother gave him some advice. "I advise you to start slowly," Ray said. "Runners who go too fast often lose their energy before the finish."

Marco nodded and bent down to check his shoes. One lace felt loose, so he pulled it tight and tied a double knot. At the starting line, he took a deep breath. The cool morning air was easy to breathe, and his nervous feelings began to fade.

The race went once around the park, a full mile. Marco remembered Ray's advice and kept an easy pace. By the halfway point, his legs ached, and he doubted he could run any farther. Then he thought further about his brother's words. If he stayed steady, he would have energy left for the end.

In the last stretch, Marco sped up and passed three runners. He crossed the line out of breath but smiling. Priya, the winner, gave him a compliment. "You ran a smart race," she said. His bright orange shirt seemed to complement the red and gold leaves behind him, and a classmate snapped a photo.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, what does the word "loose" mean?
qs.why: Marco pulled the lace tight to fix it, so it had not been tight enough.

qs.q: Which meaning of "advice" fits the first paragraph?
choices: A trick to run faster by cheating
A short break during a race
Helpful words about what to do
qs.why: Ray tells Marco what he thinks Marco should do, which is advice.

qs.q: Why did Marco keep an easy pace at the start?
choices: He trusted Ray's advice about saving energy.
He did not know where to run.
qs.why: Marco remembered Ray's advice and wanted energy left for the end.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Marco felt calmer before the race?
choices: He took a deep breath, and his nervous feelings began to fade.
He saw red and gold leaves.
qs.why: The breath and the fading nervous feelings are the signs that he calmed down.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Racing is only for older kids.
Good advice and a steady plan helped Marco run a smart race.
Priya always wins the school race.
qs.why: The story shows Marco using Ray's advice and ending with a strong, smart race.

teacher.overview: Students learn five confusable pairs by seeing them side by side. Each day pairs a spelling or sound clue with a test sentence, then moves to meaning in context. The passage uses all ten words so students must choose meaning, not only spelling.

notes.va.advice.n: Noun, rhymes with ice. Have students say the sentence aloud: if the word names words someone gives you, it is advice. Students often write advice for the verb.
notes.va.advise.v: Verb, ends with the z sound. Practice the swap test: can you replace it with suggest or recommend? If so, use advise.
notes.va.lose.v: Rhymes with choose and has one o. Students often add a second o because the word sounds long. Model a quick check: if you can swap in misplace, use lose.
notes.va.loose.adj: Extra o in the spelling, and the sound ends with s. Show a loose lace and ask students to describe the gap. Link to the antonym tight.
notes.va.farther.adv: Use for distance you can measure with a ruler or in miles. Many writers use farther and further interchangeably in everyday speech, so teach the measurable-distance rule as a helpful convention for writing.
notes.va.further.adv: Use for more, as in further questions or further study. Students may need a quick test: can I measure it? If not, further.
notes.va.breath.n: Noun with no e, ends with the th sound as in death. Show cold-day breath clouds to make it concrete.
notes.va.breathe.v: Verb with a final e, ends with the th sound as in seethe. Have students put a hand on their chest and breathe slowly while saying the word.
notes.va.compliment.n: The i in compliment can remind students of I like it. Role-play giving specific compliments, not just nice.
notes.va.complement.v: The e links to completes. Use paired colors or foods: a complement makes the other thing better or complete.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The sentence says, "A scarf will ___ her coat," and the colors match. Is this kind words or going well together? It is going well together, so I need complement with an e, like completes the outfit.'
discuss: Why do you think one letter can change a word's meaning?
Which pair is hardest for you, and what clue helps?
misconceptions: Lose and loose are different spellings of the same word.
Advice and advise can be used in the same way.
Breath and breathe are pronounced the same.
Farther and further always mean exactly the same thing.
extend: Make a poster for one pair with a picture, a spelling clue, and two sample sentences.
Search a class book for a time when a writer used advice or advise and decide whether it was correct.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit each pair with a quick test sentence two days later and again at one week. Add the four most-missed words to the editing checklist for the next writing assignment.
